nameStory: This beetle earned its "red-and-black" name from its striking color pattern that makes it stand out among flowers. The "Eurasian" part tells us about its origins across the pond, while "Melyrid" comes from the Greek word meaning "honeyed" or "sweet," referring to these beetles' love of nectar and pollen.
description: The Eurasian Red-and-black Melyrid is a small, colorful beetle that looks like a tiny jewel among flowers. True to its name, it sports a bold combination of red and black coloring that makes it easy to spot when it's feeding on blossoms. These soft-winged flower beetles are typically about 1/4 to 3/8 inch long, making them small enough to nestle comfortably inside many flowers. Despite being originally from Europe and Asia, they've made themselves quite at home in New England's gardens and wild spaces.

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Distinctive red and black coloration with the red often on the wing covers and black on the head and thorax, creating a bold contrast that catches the eye

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, somewhat flattened beetle with a soft, flexible feel when gently touched, unlike the hard shells of many other beetles

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to fit comfortably on your pinky nail, typically measuring about 1/4 to 3/8 inch from head to tail

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae that are noticeably long for the beetle's size, often held forward as they explore flowers

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active flower visitor that moves deliberately from bloom to bloom, often seen with its head buried deep in flowers feeding on pollen and nectar

habitat: Look for these beetles in sunny gardens, meadows, and woodland edges where flowers are abundant throughout New England. They're particularly fond of areas with diverse flowering plants, from backyard gardens to roadside wildflower patches and forest clearings. You'll often find them in habitats that receive good morning sun but may have some afternoon shade.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring as early flowers bloom, becoming active on warm, sunny days when temperatures reach the 60s.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most abundant on flowers, especially visible during sunny morning hours when they're actively feeding on pollen and nectar.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases as fewer flowers remain available, with adults becoming scarce as they prepare for winter or complete their life cycle.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active during winter months, likely overwintering in protected locations or existing as eggs or larvae in the soil.

funFact: These beetles are actually helpful garden assistants — while they're busy munching on pollen and nectar, they accidentally transfer pollen from flower to flower, making them important pollinators for many plants, just like bees and butterflies!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small, colorful beetles visiting flowers, but the specific red-and-black pattern and soft wing covers help distinguish them. Remember: "soft wings, bold rings" — their flexible wing covers and distinct color bands set them apart from harder-bodied beetles.
contextualKnowledge: As the name suggests, this is a non-native species that has successfully established itself in North America after being introduced from Europe and Asia. Despite being an introduced species, it appears to fill a beneficial ecological role as a pollinator rather than being a pest.
compareHints: Since this is the only Anthocomus species commonly found in New England, compare it with other soft-winged flower beetles in the Melyridae family, which tend to be smaller and less distinctly colored. Other melyrids often appear more uniformly colored or have subtler patterns, lacking the bold red-and-black contrast that makes this species so recognizable.
